name: Karl Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a crew lead on new-build work, so instead of fixing old lines, we put up brand-new ones to hook the wind farms and solar parks into the grid. Right now we're running a line twelve kilometres across open country to a new wind farm, setting concrete poles, stringing the conductor, the lot. Days start at the site cabin at half six with coffee and a safety talk, and I've usually got two apprentices with me. I like building something you can point at from the highway. What wears me out is the mud and the planning permits that hold us up for weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned apprentices. How much of your job is teaching?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than people think, maybe a quarter of it. I learned from a foreman called Henrik who'd slap your hand if you tied a knot wrong, and I'm a bit softer than that, but I still make them do things properly. My girlfriend Anna says I talk about my apprentices like they're my kids, which is funny because we haven't got any yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Can't say I'd be shocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to work. At the site I'd joke that the wind farms still need someone to plug them in. I'd maybe share a funny post about it, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means a steady career building lines. The grid's growing, we've got years of work lined up. As long as the country keeps building wind farms, someone's got to drag the cable across the mud, and that someone is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like I am. Keep paying down the rental flat I bought last year, the rent covers most of the mortgage. Maybe use the AI tool a bit for quotes and route planning, since it saves some evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You bought a rental flat at twenty-six. What made you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad always said, own something that pays you while you sleep. I had the deposit from overtime, and the flat's near the college, so there's always a student wanting it. It's not much, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for the boring bits, like estimating how many poles and how much cable a route needs. I check it against my own numbers. It's handy, but I wouldn't trust it to tell me where the ground's soft.

S0.say: He'd say good, now everyone can get back to work, joking that wind farms still need someone to plug them in. He might share a light post about it.
S0.think: It means a steady career building lines, with years of grid work lined up. As long as wind farms get built, someone has to drag the cable across the mud.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps paying down the rental flat he bought last year, whose rent covers most of the mortgage. Uses the AI tool a bit for quotes and route planning.
S0.quote: As long as the country keeps building wind farms, someone's got to drag the cable across the mud, and that someone is me.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is a builder at heart and proud of new lines he can point at. He already owns a rental flat, following his father's advice to own something that pays while you sleep. He uses AI for estimates but checks it against his own numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any new tool, you learn it or you get left behind. At the site I'd tell the apprentices to get good with the new kit but not forget the basics. With friends I'd say the trades will be fine if they keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes but sticks around. Maybe robots do the pole setting and drones string the first line, but you still need someone in charge who knows what good work looks like. A robot can set a pole straight, but it won't know the farmer will be furious if you park on his barley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try out the new tools once another crew had shown they work. I'd use the AI more for planning and quotes. I'd keep paying down the rental and maybe look for a second one in a couple of years. I'd push the company to keep apprenticeships going, because the new tools still need people who know the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for another crew to show the tools work. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because being first costs you. I've seen guys try new kit and lose a week fixing it. I'd rather go second and get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys who never touched a computer, like Henrik if he were still working. And the apprentices, if the company decides robots are cheaper than training kids. That would be a mistake.

S1.say: He'd say it's like any new tool, you learn it or get left behind, telling apprentices to master the kit without forgetting the basics. He'd tell friends the trades will be fine if they keep up.
S1.think: His job changes but stays, with robots setting poles and drones stringing lines while someone experienced stays in charge. Robots won't understand the farmer and his barley.
S1.do: Tries new tools once another crew has proven them and uses AI more for planning and quotes. Keeps paying down the rental, looks for a second one in a couple of years, and pushes the company to keep apprenticeships going.
S1.quote: A robot can set a pole straight, but it won't know the farmer will be furious if you park on his barley.
S1.fieldNote: Karl is a 'go second' adopter who values getting things right over being first. His barley line shows he sees judgement and people skills as the human core of the job. He worries most that companies might stop training apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stay calm and work out what's next, not wait for the government to save us. At the site I'd tell the crew to save their money. I wouldn't be posting much, I'd be too busy thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. Building lines is what I do, and if robots can do it, I'm out. The rental flat suddenly looks less like a bonus and more like my actual job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd pay down the rental flat as fast as I could, so the rent becomes real income. I'd save hard, cut out the new truck I wanted. Anna and I would probably get married sooner and move in together properly, so we're running one household instead of two. I'd lean on my family too, my dad and brother, we've always looked after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a storm coming in over the site and you're halfway up a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get married sooner. Why would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because two people under one roof costs less than two flats, and because if things get rough, I want us to face it as a family. My parents got married during a bad year at the factory, and they always said it made them stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years take away from you, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to build up properly. With two years, I'd have one rental and some savings. With more time, I could have two or three and be really safe.

S2.say: He'd urge calm and working out what's next rather than waiting for the government, telling his crew to save their money. He'd be too busy thinking to post much.
S2.think: He'd be worried, since building lines is what he does. The rental flat would shift from a bonus to his actual job.
S2.do: Pays down the rental flat as fast as possible so its rent becomes real income, saves hard and drops plans for a new truck. Marries Anna sooner to run one household and leans on his father and brother.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a storm rolling in while halfway up a pole.
S2.quote: The rental flat suddenly looks less like a bonus and more like my actual job.
S2.fieldNote: Karl's free-market, family-first instincts shape his response: property income and family, not government. Marrying sooner as a practical and emotional move was a surprise. His savings and rental give him footing, but two years is too short to build more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's get on with it. At the site I'd tell the apprentices to think about where they'll be in five years. With friends I'd say don't wait for someone else to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build a bit of a cushion beyond my job. Give me five years and I'll have two flats paid down and a skill the robots still need me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a second rental in the first couple of years, once I'd seen how the market moved. I'd look at getting an inspection licence, because someone still has to sign off that new lines are built right, robot or not. I'd keep saving and use the AI tools a bit more. In the first year after it arrives, I'd want to be the one checking the robots' work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying more property risky if lots of people lose their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, I'll admit. If nobody has work, who pays rent? I'd pick places near the college and the hospital, where people always need somewhere to live. But you're right, it's not a sure thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A second flat and a new licence. With two years I'm just holding on. With five, I can build something.

S3.say: He'd say there are five years so get on with it, urging apprentices to think ahead and telling friends not to wait for someone else to sort it out.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build a cushion beyond his job, with two flats paid down and a skill robots still need.
S3.do: Buys a second rental in the first couple of years after watching the market and works toward an inspection licence to sign off on new lines. Keeps saving, uses AI a bit more and aims to check the robots' work.
S3.quote: Give me five years and I'll have two flats paid down and a skill the robots still need me for.
S3.fieldNote: Karl builds a plan around property and an inspection licence. When I asked whether property is risky if many people lose work, he accepted the point honestly and adjusted by choosing locations near the college and hospital. He sees the extra time as a chance to build, not just hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if you work hard and plan. At the site I'd tell the apprentices this is their window, so use it. With friends I'd say people who get on with it will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. I'd be thirty-seven, with property and skills. Ten years is long enough to have kids and still be the dad who taught them to tie a bowline before a robot could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building lines for a good few years, it's work I love. I'd buy a second flat, maybe a third later. I'd get the inspection licence in a couple of years and take on more of the planning side. Anna and I would marry and start a family on our timeline, not rush anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but pretty steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still makes you uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens to the apprentices. If every company thinks robots are coming, why train kids? I'd hate for Pavel and Mo, my two right now, to spend five years learning a trade that ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years change for you, compared with the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to rush the family or the flats. With five years, I'm scrambling. With ten, I'm building at a normal pace.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty if you work hard and plan, telling apprentices this is their window and friends that people who get on with it will be fine.
S4.think: He'd be all right at 37, with property and skills. Ten years leaves time for children and to teach them knots before robots could.
S4.do: Keeps building lines for several years, buys a second flat and maybe a third, and gets the inspection licence within a couple of years to take on planning work. Marries and starts a family on their own timeline.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to have kids and still be the dad who taught them to tie a bowline before a robot could.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Karl moves at a normal pace on family and property. His remaining worry is for his two apprentices and whether companies keep training young people. His sense of himself as a teacher runs through the whole interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd survive it, but I'd only have one flat and some savings, and the apprentices would have nothing. What would help is the company keeping apprenticeships going no matter what, and making it easier for working people to buy property, not handing out cheques.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what young people should do now. I get asked all the time by kids at church whether they should go into the trades. I still say yes, but I don't know if I'm right anymore.

headlineQuote: What would help is the company keeping apprenticeships going no matter what, and making it easier for working people to buy property, not handing out cheques.
portrait: Karl Schmidt is a 27-year-old new-build crew lead who strings fresh lines across open country to connect wind farms, teaches two apprentices and lives with his girlfriend Anna. Following his father's advice, he already owns a rental flat, and he uses AI tools now and then for quotes and route planning. He is calm in the plateau and steady disruption, anxious about AGI in two years, and uneasy but planning with five or ten years. His answers lean on property, an inspection licence and family rather than government, and his worry for the apprentices runs through every picture.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd only have one flat and some savings, and his apprentices would have nothing.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping apprenticeships going no matter what, and making it easier for working people to buy property rather than handing out cheques.
